critic_changes: All five cited pages were opened (as PDFs, with the text extracted). Every quoted passage, URL, publisher and date matched the documents: IMF CR 05/98 (March 2005), IMF CR 08/336 (October 2008), IMF GFS Note 2023/001 (December 2023), IMF GFSR April 2024 ch. 2, and the OECD profile (last updated 5 July 2024). The 2008 report was completed on 8 September 2008 but dated October 2008, so 2008-10 is kept.

Arc: replaced 'IMF assessments link this [1998-2007 growth] to waves of insurance capital'. The 2005 report ties the post-2001 hard market only to growth in the Bermudian insurance market, not the whole economy. The arc now says the IMF describes the two waves of capital and ties the 2006 jump in growth to the second.

Thread 'Capital that follows disasters': the text said the IMF ties 'the island's growth in the early 2000s' to the post-2001 market. That claim was narrowed to what the 2005 and 2008 reports support. Added a 2008 IMF passage that names both waves of capital directly.

Thread 'One center carries the economy': dropped 'with tourism second', which no cited passage supports. Dropped the inference that income per person rose with insurance capital. The text now stays with what the passages say about output and jobs. The 2005 quote was lengthened to keep the page's 'with the exception of 2001' (24 words), so the jobs claim is not overstated.

Thread 'Private equity's life reinsurers': 'Large private equity firms have set up life reinsurers' was corrected to the GFSR's wording (life insurers influenced by private equity set up reinsurers). Added a GFS Note passage that supports the claim that the valuation rules gave insurers an incentive to move business to Bermuda.

Thread 'Tighter oversight': made the vague 'consulted on changes to how firms may value their liabilities' match the GFS Note. The note says the BMA consulted on requiring prior approval of the scenario-based valuation approach. Added that passage as a citation.
Thread 'A base with no income tax': removed 'only', which read more into the OECD passage than it says. Removed 'the' before 'taxable periods' in the OECD quote to match the page.

Tension: 'investment was low at 11.7 percent of GDP' now says 'low for an economy at its income', which matches the data file's comparison. 'No matching recovery' became 'no full recovery', since income per person did grow in 2021 to 2024. Note that 11.7 is the value printed in growth_problem, while series NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS shows 11.0 for 2024. The printed growth_problem figure is kept.

growth_story.headline: Bermuda's income per person rose with waves of insurance capital to a 2007 peak, fell until 2015, and in 2024 was still 12.1 percent below that peak.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 income per person in Bermuda grew slowly, at 0.8 percent a year. From 1998 to 2007 growth picked up to 3.4 percent a year, and income per person peaked in 2007. IMF assessments describe waves of new insurance capital that came to the island after the September 2001 attacks and the 2005 hurricanes, and tie the jump in growth in 2006 to the second wave. From 2008 to 2015 income per person fell by 2.9 percent a year on average, and the sources we found do not explain this slump in detail. Since 2016 growth has averaged 1.3 percent a year: a fall of 7.4 percent in 2020, then gains of 4.3, 6.1 and 4.4 percent in 2021 to 2023. Even so, income per person in 2024 was still 12.1 percent below its 2007 peak, about where it first was in 2001.

threads.title: Capital that follows disasters
threads.text: Big insured losses cut the supply of cover and push up insurance prices, and new capital then flows to Bermuda to write that business. The IMF describes such waves after September 2001 and after the 2005 hurricanes, and ties Bermuda's faster growth in 2006 to the capital that arrived after those hurricanes.

threads.title: Private equity's life reinsurers
threads.text: Life insurers tied to private equity firms have set up reinsurers in Bermuda, and long-term reinsurance assets on the island grew fast in the years to 2021. The IMF says Bermuda's more generous way of valuing these firms' liabilities has given life insurers a reason to send business there.

threads.title: A base with no income tax
threads.text: Many insurers first came to Bermuda partly because firms could set up quickly and paid no income tax. An OECD tax profile updated in July 2024 says Bermuda has no corporate income tax for tax periods up to and including 2024.

growth_story.tension: The IMF sources describe Bermuda's insurance center growing fast, with life reinsurance assets on the island rising sharply in the years to 2021. The data show no full recovery at home: income per person in 2024 was still 12.1 percent below its 2007 peak, and investment was 11.7 percent of GDP, low for an economy at its income. More assets booked in Bermuda have not brought income per person back to its peak.
